pages.text: The Coding Club

image.note: Cover: children at laptops, a game maze on screen

pages.text: Contents. The Club Begins / Learning to Code / The Big Idea / The Bug / The Hunt / Demo Day.

The game would not work. Etim pressed the key again, and again, and the little figure on the screen just stood there, blinking, refusing to move. "Come ON," he groaned, and behind him a calm voice said, "Ah. Now the real coding begins. Anyone can write it. The clever part is finding out why it will not run." That was Aunty Zainab.

image.note: Etim frustrated at a laptop, Aunty Zainab behind him

pages.text: It had started three weeks before, when a notice went up in the estate lobby: CODING CLUB. SATURDAYS. COMMUNITY ROOM. ALL WELCOME. Aunty Zainab, home from the university where she studied computers, had decided the children of Tafiya Estate should learn to make things, not just play them.

image.note: The coding club notice in the lobby

pages.text: Etim was first through the door. He loved games, and had always wondered how they worked, what was hiding behind the screen that made a character jump or a coin spin. "Everything you see," said Aunty Zainab, opening a laptop, "someone told the computer to do, step by step, in a language it understands. That language is called code. And by the end of these Saturdays, you will speak it."

image.note: Etim eager at the front, a laptop open

pages.text: The community room filled up: Etim, and Idara, who was younger and small and quiet, and a handful of others. Aunty Zainab gave each a laptop and a grin. "A computer," she said, "is not clever. It is fast, and it is obedient, and it does exactly what you tell it. Which means every mistake it makes, you made first. That is the first rule of coding."

image.note: Children at laptops in the community room

pages.text: They began with small things. Make the cat move right. Make it say hello. Make it spin when you press the space bar. Block by block, line by line, the children learned to give the computer orders it would obey. When Etim made his cat turn a somersault, he shouted so loud that Remigius looked in from the gate.

image.note: Etim's cat doing a somersault on screen

pages.text: Little Idara said almost nothing, but she watched everything. While the others rushed ahead, she read each line twice, slowly, as if listening to it. "You are careful," Aunty Zainab told her kindly. Idara only nodded. She did not know yet that being careful would, one Saturday soon, save the whole club.

image.note: Quiet Idara reading her screen carefully

pages.text: "Now," said Aunty Zainab, when they could all make a cat dance, "we build something real. A game. Your own game, made by you." The room buzzed. A game of their very own! At once everyone had an idea, and everyone's idea was the best, and nobody agreed with anybody. It was, Aunty Zainab said, a very normal start.

image.note: Excited children all talking at once

pages.text: Two big ideas rose above the rest. Etim wanted a maze, where a hungry mouse ran through twisting walls to find the cheese. But a girl named Fati wanted a quiz, where the player answered questions to win points. "Maze," said Etim. "Quiz," said Fati. Neither would budge, and the club split neatly in two.

image.note: Etim and Fati arguing, the club divided

pages.text: They argued all through snack time, until Aunty Zainab clapped her hands. "Why," she said, "choose? The best coders do not fight over two ideas. They find the one idea hiding inside both." The room went quiet. Etim looked at Fati. Fati looked at Etim. And slowly, the same grin spread across both their faces.

image.note: Etim and Fati suddenly grinning at each other

pages.text: "A maze," said Etim slowly, "where every door is locked..." "...and to open it, you answer a question!" finished Fati. It was perfect. A mouse in a maze, a question at every turn, cheese for the clever. They called it Brain Maze, and the whole club, united again, set to work to build it, room by room, question by question.

image.note: The club building Brain Maze together

pages.text: For three Saturdays Brain Maze grew, and it was glorious. The mouse scampered, the doors opened, the questions popped up, the cheese gleamed. They were almost ready for the great moment: Demo Day, when the whole estate would be invited to play. Then, the Saturday before, disaster struck.

image.note: The game working beautifully, proud kids

pages.text: They opened the game, and the mouse would not move. Not left, not right, not anywhere. It sat in the first room, blinking, while the children pressed every key on every laptop. The game they had built for weeks was frozen solid, and Demo Day was six days away. "We broke it," wailed Fati. "How? It worked yesterday!"

image.note: The frozen mouse, panic on the kids' faces

pages.text: That was when Aunty Zainab said her favourite thing. "Nothing is broken. Something is only doing exactly what you told it, which is not what you meant. That is a bug. And finding a bug," she said, rolling up her sleeves, "is the truest test of a coder. We do not guess. We hunt."

image.note: Aunty Zainab rolling up her sleeves, calm

pages.text: So they hunted. They read the code aloud, line by line, room by room, looking for the one small mistake among thousands of correct ones. It was slow, and hard, and by the fourth Saturday tempers were short and hope was thin. Etim rubbed his eyes. "It could be anywhere," he groaned. "We will never find it."

image.note: Tired children poring over lines of code

pages.text: But someone had been reading, quietly, all along. Little Idara, who never rushed, who always read each line twice, put up one small hand. "Here," she said. "Room one. You told the mouse to move when the door is open. But you told the door to open when the mouse moves. So the mouse waits for the door, and the door waits for the mouse. And nobody ever goes first."

image.note: Idara pointing at the exact line, others leaning in

pages.text: There was a long silence. Then Aunty Zainab laughed out loud and clapped Idara on the shoulder. "That," she said, "is the whole bug, found by the one who read most carefully. Two things each waiting for the other. Change one line, so the mouse may move first, and..." Etim changed it, with a trembling finger, and pressed the key.

image.note: Etim changing the line, everyone holding their breath

pages.text: The mouse moved. It ran, quick and sure, right up to the first locked door, and the first question popped up, bright and ready. The room exploded. They hugged, they cheered, they lifted little Idara clean off her feet, the quiet girl who had beaten a bug that stumped them all. Brain Maze was alive again, one day before Demo Day.

image.note: The mouse running, the club erupting in joy

pages.text: On Demo Day the community room was packed: parents, neighbours, Remigius, even Baba Danladi from the block next door. One by one they played Brain Maze, groaning at the questions, cheering the cheese, and every single one asked the same thing: "The children made this? Themselves?" They had. Every room, every question, every line.

image.note: The estate crowd playing Brain Maze

pages.text: "Who taught you?" a parent asked Etim. "Aunty Zainab," he said. "But she made us find our own mistakes." "And who found the big one?" "Idara," said the whole club at once, and small quiet Idara went warm with pride, which for once she did not mind at all.

image.note: The club pointing proudly at Idara

pages.text: As the room emptied, Aunty Zainab gathered the club. "You learned to code," she said. "But you learned something better. That the loudest idea is not always the best, that two ideas can become one, and that the careful, quiet worker often sees what the quick, clever one misses. Remember that, long after you forget the code."

image.note: Aunty Zainab addressing the proud club

pages.text: They did not forget. Brain Maze lived on the community laptop for years, and children not yet born when it was made would one day play it, and groan at the questions, and never know that once, for one terrible week, a mouse and a door sat waiting for each other, until a quiet girl read the code twice.

image.note: A younger child playing Brain Maze years later

pages.text: The Coding Club. Aunty Zainab, who taught them to hunt their own mistakes. Etim, who wanted a maze. Fati, who wanted a quiz. And Idara, quiet and careful, who found the bug that beat them all. First rule of coding: the computer does exactly what you tell it, so every mistake is yours to find.
